utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 30th of March, 2008 [as interpreted]. I would like to greet the accused, the Defence counsel, the entire OTP, the witness, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I shall first give the floor to our Registrar, who has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Makar, Andjelko. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 970, the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC971, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC972. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a minor correction to make. On page 1, line 15, we are today, the 30th of March, 2009. We are all a year older, as of now. The Trial Chamber would also like to ask the parties to give their views on the Stojic Defence team that has asked for two documents to be tendered, two documents that were not mentioned on their 65 ter list. So you have until 1900 hours to let us know whether you object to this, given that the Defence team of Mr. Stojic has asked that you have this done. This relates to the witness who has been proofed and who will be coming next Wednesday to testify. So let me know whether there are any objections to the mentioning of these two documents on the 65 ter list. Sir, could you stand, please, to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt at this stage. Just before we commence with the witness, the Prosecution would just like to briefly place a continuing objection on the record. Last week, the Trial Chamber did rule on the Prosecution's motion to exclude the irrelevant evidence of Mr. Milos, Mario, and certainly the Prosecution does accept that ruling, Your Honour. Having said that, the Prosecution does wish to reiterate that the shipment by Croatia of arms to or from the ABiH at some times and in some locations is not disputed. Testimony on this issue, therefore, does not relate to or advance the search for the truth as to any issue in dispute. The Prosecution therefore wishes to place on record its continuing objection to this irrelevant evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the record. Witness, can I have your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mario Milos. The 6th of May, 1967. Grude, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work for the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a court of law on those events that unfolded?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first testimony before any court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Sir, we'll try and be brief. Ms. Nozica has told you, undoubtedly, that there will be no hearing tomorrow because of the international conference that will be held next-door to this building, so if we can finish your testimony today, this means that you will not have to wait until next Wednesday. Ms. Nozica, I'm sure, has told you how things work here. She will put questions to you and show you a series of documents that are contained in this binder, and you will answer those questions that are put to you. After that, the other Defence lawyers who are sitting next to her or behind her will also put questions to you, and the Prosecutor, sitting on your right-hand side, will have the same time as Ms. Nozica to put questions to you. The Judges before you may also put questions to you on the basis of those documents that we have before us. Please try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer those questions. If there is a question that you do not understand, do not hesitate to ask the person who has put you that question to rephrase it. I hope you have understood me well. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. Before I commence, I would like to inform the Chamber that given the statement made by the OTP today at the outset, and in order to make a complete statement, given the importance of this statement, I can only say that my chief will take no more than one and a half hours. Perhaps I can even make it shorter. Given the nature of the statement, I think we can speed things along a little, and I expect that we shall be finishing our chief during our sitting today. If I manage to do that, we could still remain in keeping with the schedule for this week, in view of the fact that we are not sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milos.

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to go through your personal details quickly. Please just confirm at the end whether everything is true. You were born in Grude in 1969, as you said. It was in Zagreb that you completed a school for the commerce?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. August 1991, I joined the TO for the east of Zagreb city, Zesveta [phoen]. Up until September, I remained there. In September, I started working with the security of the ordnance storage in Duboki Jarak until December 1991, when I started working with the Croatian Army on a regular basis as a storage-keeper in Duboki Jarak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Mario, can I just ask you one thing? We need to pause between my questions and your answers, just to make sure that everything is recorded properly. You will have to wait for me until I complete my question before you start answering. One thing that I wish to say is -- or, rather, as you have said yourself, you were working in the Duboki Jarak storage unit. In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: I was the manager of that storage unit, the storage unit keeper. I was in charge of issuing MTS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you go too much into the merits, the witness told the President, and that's what's recorded, that he was born in 1967; and you have told him that he was born in 1969, and it is not possible that both apply. It would be very extraordinary. So, Witness, were you born in 1967 or in 1969, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I'm sure you have proof of this rectification.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My note, too, reads "1967." I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, you said you were working in the storage unit as the foreman or the manager; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was this a JNA storage unit or warehouse before the Croatian Army occupied this area?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. It used to be a JNA storage unit, and then there was a broader operation in the Republic of Croatia, and the East Zagreb Territorial Defence took all the warehouse and storage units belonging at that point in time to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What exactly was in this storage unit when the Croatian Army took the storage unit?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Ordnance and MTS. We drew up lists immediately after entering the storage unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What exactly was your job in this warehouse, this storage unit, from the moment you came there?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: My job was to issue MTS, depending on its type and the amount that was specified on requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe to the Chamber what sort of procedure was applied whenever MTS was issued? Which bodies were in charge of what in terms of preliminaries for MTS to be issued?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: All those who received equipment and who were supposed to pick up MTS would get an order from Croatia's Defence Ministry. They would take this order or request and go to the Technical and Traffic Department of the Defence Ministry, and then based on that order they would write up a request. They would then take that request and see me about equipment. The Technical and Traffic Administration had a complete list covering the situation and the amounts available in our storage unit and in all storage units across the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you just try to slow down a little bit, please. Thank you. The Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia would issue an order, if my understanding is correct, and then the Technical and Traffic Administration would issue a request; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What exactly would eventually reach you? What did you get? What was the name of the document that you received in your capacity as the manager of that storage unit?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: What I received was the request issued by the Technical and Traffic Department specifying exactly who was taking delivery and the name of the person who was in charge of the equipment, of receiving or taking delivery of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what was it that you would issue in return, what sort of document, while issuing equipment?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: We would issue a receipt to confirm that equipment was issued. The place was recorded where the goods were issued; the kind, type, and amount of MTS issued would be specified; the first and last names of the person taking delivery or receiving equipment, normally the driver; as well as the plate number of the vehicle onto which MTS was loaded. Obviously, our own names, whoever it was that was in charge of issuing MTS, would also be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about you and the person receiving equipment; would you not both sign this receipt?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: No, the receiving person would sign the receipts. Normally, there were other persons with the drivers who had their own orders and were in charge of receiving equipment, but they didn't sign for it. It was the drivers who signed, and then there was normally a document attached specifying that they were the ones who were in charge of taking delivery.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How long did this procedure continue for? First, there was an order. Then there was a request. Finally, there was a receipt, as you've just described. Was the procedure applied throughout your time at the storage unit?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: No. This procedure continued until the end of 1992, and then the procedure was computerised. The Technical and Traffic Administration introduced computer-generated receipts replacing both requests and receipts, so now we no longer drew up a receipt. We would simply record our own personal details; first name, last name, goods issued, as well as amounts, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, what other storage units were there, for example, in the broader Zagreb area where MTS was kept?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: In Zagreb itself, there was Popovic [phoen] that was part of Duboki Jarak, and we were in charge of that storage unit too. It was a subordinate storage unit, as it were. There was also the Precko storage unit. There was Varazdin Breg in Varazdin at Precac at Ivinic Grad. Those were the storage units that were directly under the central storage unit of the Defence Ministry. If I may just add, there were other storage units or warehouses across the Republic of Croatia, but I didn't know much about those other storage units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Milos, what about you and your storage unit? Was MTS issued for the purposes of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will have an opportunity to look at some receipts for MTS from your warehouse. Can you please tell us, based on your own recollection, who were the storage-keepers in your storage unit?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Mirsad Malagic, Mario Juricin [phoen], Vukasic [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Slowly, please, because everything is being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Mirsad Malagic --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: One at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name? There was overlap. We didn't hear the name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Niksa Puharic , Marin Kohososter [phoen], and me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can we now please go through a number of documents that I've prepared. We're looking at orders, the orders that you talked about that came from the Defence Ministry. You have a binder in front of you, or, rather, do you? Does the witness have the binder?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: A binder, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Could you please have a look. 2D956, that's the first one up. Tell me as soon as you've got it.

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber, is this the kind of order that you talked about? This was the step before any MTS was issued. This was the first step-order issued by the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the sort of order drawn up by Croatia's Defence Ministry. They would have forwarded this to us. There is mention here of Mr. Bilic. He was one of the people working for the Technical and Traffic Administration. The Technical and Traffic Administration would receive an order like this, and then based on an order like this, they would write up a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Based on this order, Mr. Milos, can we see who the MTS was for?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This MTS was for the BH Army. It is stated here that Mr. Fehim Nuhbegovic, whom I happen to know as the chief logistician of the BH Army, and he was the one who most frequently came with any of the drivers to pick up equipment. Therefore, it is quite beyond doubt, at least to my mind, that this was for the purposes of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next one is P231. That should be the next document in your binder. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another order dated the 29th of May, 1992. Looking at this order, can we see who the equipment was for? Who was supposed to get it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This is identical to the previous one. Again, Mr. Bilik [phoen] was supposed to get this directly. He was a man from the Technical and Traffic Administration, and we can also see that Mr. Fehim Nuhbegovic would be taking delivery, the logistician of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document, P00238. Can you comment on this, please? Another order, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, another one drawn up by the Defence Ministry, again, Mr. Vragotuk, who was the head of the Technical and Traffic Administration. Likewise, we see that delivery was taken by Mr. Fehim Nuhbegovic. Therefore, there is no doubt the equipment was for the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next one, P262. Your comment, please. Is this the same --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could there be a pause between questions and answers, and could speakers please not speak at the same time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Ms. Nozica. Really, the interpreters have already at least five times asked you and the witness to slow down and to wait between questions and answers, so please try to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, please, just a little, a little, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Chamber. I have only now seen the reference to this in the transcript, and I was just about to caution the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, looking at an order like this, can you tell us if some equipment, for example, the equipment specified in the order before us, could originate from the Duboki Jarak storage unit, which was your own storage unit, and how was the decision taken as to which particular storage unit any of these requests would eventually be sent?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Quite a few of these articles were in our depot at the time. The decision as to from what depot goods would be issued was taken by the Technical and Traffic Administration, which knew what the situation was in each depot, so it was they who decided from which depot particular MTS would be taken and who would be authorised to take delivery of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the last document of this type is P00267. Is this the same kind of document?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same kind of document. It's the same sort of request, and to Mr. Vragotuk, the chief of the Technical and Traffic Administration; and the same gentleman, Fehim Nuhbegovic, is taking delivery of the MTS, which means the MTS was being issued for the needs of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, to sum up what has been said so far, you explained that the Technical and Traffic Administration, after receiving an order from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, drew up a request which arrived in the depot, or any depot, and based on that request, persons working in the depot issued receipts. I will now show you a certain number of these receipts, asking you to comment on who drew them up and to whom the MTS was issued. Now, please look at 2D951, 2D951, and then we will comment on what is mentioned in this document. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at record of issued items number 240. Are these records of issued items which were filled in in the depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. And from this record of issued items, one can see that the goods came from the Duboki Jarak depot. I haven't seen this number yet of the request, but the record of issued items is number 240. It bears the date when the MTS was issued. Aziz Milkic received the goods. He was one of the drivers, and one can see that the license plate of the vehicle is from Travnik, and the goods were issued by Niksa Puharic. You can see his signature here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To whom was this MTS issued, or for whom was it intended?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Well, it went to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please look at the next record of issued items. It's number 242. Can you comment on which warehouse employee signed it, to whom the goods were issued, and for whom they were intended? So tell me those three pieces of information in the case of each record.

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: It was Niksa Puharic who issued the goods. Nermin Arnautovic took delivery, and this went to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps the Trial Chamber will find it strange that it says that the vehicle was HV, an HV vehicle, but very often the BH Army had poor vehicles, vehicles which were not in good condition, and they were not registered. The Croatian Army would allow them to have a temporary license plate on their vehicles in order to be able to transport the goods to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, while you were working in the warehouse, did you get to know most of these drivers who worked for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the persons who were tasked with taking delivery of the MTS?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them all. I knew Mr. Fehim Nuhbegovic, Seta Sujab. They were the only logistics men. The others were just drivers, but we knew almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now look at record 242 -- oh, I think we've just seen it and that you've commented on it, so let's go on to number 245. It's a record of issued items, and the number of it is 245. And can you comment on it briefly?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. I issued this MTS. It was for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Mirsad Milkic took delivery.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did these goods go to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next record of issued items is number 419. Let's go through this more quickly and look at 419, 422, 424, and 423. Have you seen all of these records of issued items, and can you say whether the MTS was issued from your depot for the needs of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. All this MTS was issued for the needs of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at record of issued items 425, 439, 447, 505, 506, 511, and 512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt my learned colleague, but I note that there are two records numbered 419, and I wonder which one was actually being referred to, or perhaps both. They're separated by number 422, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 419, to clarify, and we can see it on the screen. Maybe in your folder it has not been put in good order, but 419 is 2D530063. 0063 are the last numbers, and I think we have it in e-court now. It's followed by 422, which is 2D530064; and the next one is 424, which is 2D530065. And in the break, if my learned friend agrees, we can check whether something has been printed erroneously, but they're now all in order, and to avoid wasting time we can clarify this further during the break. Thank you. I do apologise. I think -- excuse me, Witness. Let me just check where we left off. I think the last one was -- well, there was 447, so please take a look at 505, and then all the way to 512, 518, 524, 531, 533. We'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that all these records of issued items were issued in your depot and that all this MTS went to the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: All these records of issued items were issued in Duboki Jarak. They were signed by me and my colleague. We were working in the warehouse at the time, and all the MTS went to the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milos, did you yourself write out and sign record 533?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at 534, 536, 537, 538, 539, 542, 545, 546, and 572. Can you confirm again that all these records of issued items referred to goods issued from your depot and that all this MTS was for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. All these records of issued items were written out in the Duboki Jarak depot, and all this MTS went to the BH Army. It was signed by warehouse employees who were my colleagues working in the depot with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, please look at the next record of issued items. It's number 37, and the page number is 2D530087. In the English version, it's 750060. Please explain to Their Honours when these records of issued items were written out, and were such records also issued from your depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This is a new type of record. As I explained earlier, it was done according to a computer file sent from the administration of the Technical and Traffic Administration, and we only signed who had issued the goods, who had received them, and what quantities had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, the record of issued items number 37 refers to goods issued from Precko. Is that from your depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: No, no. The depot in Precko is part of the base, and I know Mr. Sovic [phoen]. I know quite a few of these warehouse employees personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next one is number 47, and we can see that there are two versions. The lower one is signed. The amount of MTS is the same, and it was issued in Precec, Ivanic Grad. That's not your depot, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: No, it's not the one I worked in, but it was part of the logistics base of the central warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the next page is 56 and 48. Can you confirm that this is from your depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: No, this is from Precec, Ivanic Grad. It was signed by Mr. Dominko Srecko. I know him personally, and you can see here that the document was certified by Military Post Precec, 1085/15 Precec.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, I want you to tell us whether this new form of record of issued items, used in all warehouses as of the end of 1992, is this it?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at two more documents about the same topic; that is, the new form of record. 960, 2D960, that's the next document in your bundle. Mr. Milos, is this the sort of electronic record that was created at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. After 1992 onwards, this is what they looked like, and we can see the date here is 1993, so this is an example of a computer-generated record of issued items.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And could you please look at document 2D961. This is a record of issued items of the 8th of March, 1993, again from Precec Ivanic Grad, and in this record it says that the goods were taken over by Seta Sujab. Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, as I knew Mr. Fehim Nuhbegovic. They were the ones who usually came with their drivers to take delivery of the goods. They were logistics men of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, to transport the MTS that were issued, was any form of approval necessary? Were you shown such letters of approval by the drivers?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. The drivers would arrive with approval issued by the Ministry of the Interior to transport dangerous goods, a permit to drive through the Republic of Croatia. They would also have a certificate issued by the SIS Administration for the route they were taking.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at some of -- this type of document, 2D197, please. This was issued in 1993, on the 15th of March, by the SIS Administration of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Is this the sort of approval that the drivers had to have when transporting MTS?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example of what those certificates looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We see here that in this certificate of approval, it says that MTS for the needs of the BH Army Centre for Logistics in Visoko is to be transported; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the leader of the convoy is listed. Did you have information to the effect that if there was more than one driver, one was designated leader of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes one person and sometimes several would be listed as those escorting or leading the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, 2D529. The 2nd of March is the date on that document. It's an SIS certificate from the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia, an SIS certificate approving a transport of equipment for the purposes of the BH Army. That's how it reads. Are we talking about the sort of certificates that the SIS would issue, and then you knew that the drivers and the convoy leaders transporting MTS for the BH Army had those on them?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This is one of the certificates. It's not only that I knew about those. I actually saw drivers and convoy escorts carry these certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another one, 2D531. Is this the same type, the 8th of March, 1993, the same type of certificate as the previous ones?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same type, but you see, at the end it says attached to the certificate, when being checked, a MUP decision. What I told you previously about the MUP decision, this certificate shows that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the MUP decision; not this specific one, but another one that we've been able to locate. This is 2D00959. That's the decision. Is this the sort of MUP decision that you spoke about? Tell us what you know about this. What was the reason for these decisions? Why were they issued?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This is a MUP decision. It says the Fire and Explosion Protection Department, so every time there was ordnance being transported with the Republic of Croatia or any explosives at all, there was a law that said how much could be transported and who was allowed to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The decision says exactly what you suggest. This is the Fire and Explosion Protection Department. We see the driver's names there. Can we please look at the next document which links up with this one, 2D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have not said anything so far, but I have something to say to this document that was made on the 3rd of August, 1993. Earlier on, we saw a lot of documents dating back to 1992 and March 1993. Here we have a document dated in August. As far as you know, since you were a store-keeper, so far as you can remember, throughout 1993 did Croatia delivery weapons, munitions, and various other types of equipment to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At your level -- you were an ordinary store-keeper. I think you were a sergeant, that was your rank, but sergeants do think too. So at your level, when Croatia would send weapons throughout the year 1993, did it send weapons to a friendly army or to an enemy, hostile army, or don't you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know who on earth would have the idea of feeding their own enemy or who would think of providing one's own enemy with weapons to then end up killing you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, from now on if the Chamber asks you any questions, or anyone else in the courtroom, please provide direct answers. It is not the usual practice to answer a question by asking another question, although we all understand what you mean. Mr. Milos, do you know if the BH Army had their own logistics bases in Croatia, any that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: I heard the drivers talking, or the gentlemen who came to pick up the equipment, about their bases in Croatia, but I -- I didn't know their exact locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We shall now be skipping a document and looking at 2D528. If you can please tell the Chamber about this. This is a document, an authorisation. This is 2D528. You have it on your screen, if you can't find it in the binder: Authorisation signed by the Main Staff, the Zagreb Operative Zone Command, the Logistics Sector, authorising Mr. Hasan Rizvic, throughout the territory of the Republic of Croatia, to transport the following MTS. We've come across this name before, Hasan Rizvic. Did that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was he taking delivery of this MTS on behalf of?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: For the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you have many times now given the answer that the MTS that was given out by you went to the ABiH Army. Do you know more precisely where they went, in which areas geographically, or is that something that was not mentioned and did not enter in your domain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no way we could know that. The BH Army is the BH Army. Where they were, where they had their own locations, that was up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Authorisation, authorising Mr. Hasan Rizvic to transport the following MTS in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Milos, my question would be: Did you know anything about the BH Army taking delivery of MTS from anyone else, other than directly from your depot or other similar depots across Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: What this document shows is that the BH Army probably continued to take delivery from other military districts, as well, that were not directly under the HQ. They were getting equipment from another base, obviously. They were receiving assistance from all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please look at 2D00962. Have you got that? Mr. Milos, what we see here is a list of equipment itemised for the BH Army, 1993. And then after that, there is an overview of equipment issued to the BH Army in 1993, artillery and rocket ammunition, infantry weapons and infantry ammunition. Can you please look at receipt number 740, which is attached. This is 7.62 cartridge or bullets, a million of those. And after that, receipt 288, another receipt issued by your own depot, Duboki Jarak, on the 13th March, 1993. The previous one was the 26th of March, 1993. Can you tell us who signed receipt 288? Did this come from your own depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: This was signed by Mr. Mirsad Malagic, who was one of the people working in my depot. He was one of the keepers. The equipment came from Duboki Jarak. You can tell the amounts: Rocket-launcher mines, 547; Maljutka rockets, 50 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at receipt 763, which is the last one in this document. Equipment taken from Precko; right? Seta Sujab taking delivery. The date is the 13th of May, 1993. 7.62, 3 million cartridges. I'm asking you all these questions, Mr. Milos, for the following reason: The first overview of equipment issued to the BH Army in 1993 was produced based on these three receipts. Do you know whether other equipment was issued, aside from the equipment recorded in the overview for 1993 for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the unnecessary microphones be switched off, please. We can't hear anyone from the background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's obvious that someone tried to do something here, but I don't think this amount is accurate. The quantities here are too low. We provided a lot more than that for the purposes of the BH Army. I think we saw some receipts from 1993 that -- well, we've gone through some, and the amounts are reflected there, but I don't see them here. I don't see them recorded anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, we have gone through those. Can we now please go to 2D960, and then we'll be going back to those two receipts. But this is supposed to be the next receipt. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is 128, receipt 128. This receipt, as well, dates the 8th of March, 1993; is that right, Mr. Milos?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether this amount of ammunition, generally speaking, was in fact included in the overview that we looked at a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Well, it's evident the 52-millimetre cartridge is unmarked. It's an artillery piece. It's not an infantry piece, but the quantity is not reflected there, and it's simply unmarked, not marked as having been issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Rather, to be perfectly accurate, if we look at 2D962, we don't find the quantity recorded there. 2D960 shows that the equipment was, in fact, issued in 1993; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another document of the same type, 2D961. Again, receipt 133, the 8th of March, 1993; delivery taken by Seta Sujab, as we've seen before. Mr. Milos, can you please confirm whether this quantity of bullets was recorded in the previous document, 2D962, and that was the overview of equipment issued to the BH Army in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: I can confirm that this was not recorded. If you go back to that document, you'll see that information simply wasn't recorded. It wasn't included, these quantities that were effectively issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Milos, what about your own depot in Duboki Jarak? Were the requests that you spoke about also kept there, and all the accompanying documents, including orders and then requests? Was that kept or stored anywhere in your depot? Have you ever seen that?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: We kept all of the requests that we received, as well as any of our receipts. We would previously fax those and report to the Technical and Traffic Administration, specifying what equipment was issued and how much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what became of your depot? Is it still around? How long was it around for, being used as a military depot?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: The depot was blown up in the explosion in April 1994. All of the documents were destroyed in the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Milos. Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much. I would also like to thank my colleague for his statement at the outset because that greatly reduced the time that I required for examining this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, I have a very short follow-up question for you. The documents issued state that in 1992-1993, the Republic of Croatia provided various material, equipment, arms, and ammunition to the ABiH. As far as you know, were these materials a military secret, or did everyone in Croatia know about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think nearly everyone knew, although it was supposed to be classified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see which Defence counsel would like to take the floor now. Who shall we start with? D6, Mr. Ibrisimovic? What about D1?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D3?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several times yourself, and I looked at the receipts, too, quite frequently there is a reference to Seta Sujab, but another name, Fehim Nuhbegovic, as people who took delivery. You said that they were the BH Army logisticians who were involved; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes, than's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you knew where those people were staying whenever they came to a place?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Probably somewhere in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they did not travel every day in a convoy; they were actually staying in the country as far as you know; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were staying in their own logistics bases that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. Were they civilians or military personnel working for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: Probably military. I don't think they would have allowed civilians to transport weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: There were rumours circulating among the depot-keepers, so that's why I'm asking. Witness, did you perhaps know that anywhere in Zagreb, Precko, or someplace like that, there were places where weapons were being placed in cans for the purposes of the BH Army? Cans were opened and then emptied and filled with bullets, that sort of thing, and then were smuggled; anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARIO MILOS
utterances.text: That was the story. I don't know whether that was actually true or not. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Petkovic has no questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best would be to have the break now, and then we shall begin with the cross-examination after the break. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may indicate at this stage already, the Prosecution also has no cross-examination for this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, Witness, you have understood that your testimony has now come to a close, so the Prosecutor has no questions for you. The Judges have put their questions. There will be no redirect, since there is no cross-examination. So I would like to thank you for having come at the request of Mr. Stojic's Defence counsel to contribute your testimony on the delivery of weapons. I wish you a safe journey home. I would like to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone else. I can inform the Trial Chamber that in respect of the Stojic Defence request to add two exhibits to its 65 ter list for the next witness, the Prosecution has no objection to that. And also, I have one request, which is in respect to the last witness, Mr. Makar. Because of the suspension or the fact that we're not working tomorrow and the fact that we are coming back, then, first thing in the morning on Wednesday to continue the trial, it's our request if we could have an extra one day to prepare and to submit our responses to the two IC documents that were submitted just today by the two Defence teams. We'd be grateful if we could just file our response to those on Thursday morning, first thing, instead of Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it assists, there is no objection on behalf of the Stojic Defence to that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has borne in mind that no one can come and work tomorrow, so it is quite legitimate for the Prosecution to have time to reply. Therefore, Mr. Stringer, you will have until Thursday to file your written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago, as far as those two documents are concerned which Mr. Stringer does not object to, I don't have the view of the other Defence teams. We have until 7.00 p.m., but it would probably be better if it's until 5.00 p.m. today. If you could give us your positions orally, we would gain some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have conferred, and I don't think any Defence has any objections to raise about those two documents being listed as 65 ter documents of the Stojic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since we have some time on our hands, I wanted to indicate to Mr. Praljak's Defence team that the Prosecutor has filed written submissions concerning a number of witness summaries. The Prosecution has broken these down one item after the other. Please, if you could respond to the written submissions of the Prosecution. I know that you're not starting tomorrow to hear your witnesses, but I think it might be useful to look into this. There are comments which are several pages long which have been submitted by the Prosecution, so please review these and respond to the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber would like to be advised of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We had intended to submit our response today or tomorrow, but we still don't have all the required information. So if there is no obstacle, I would prefer to wait for a day or two. However, we will respond by the end of the week at the latest and maybe sooner. Otherwise, we run the risk of having to amend our response with information received subsequently. If we can wait until the end of the week, our information will be precise and we will not need to make any amendments or modifications to our response, so it will simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a personal question regarding your written submissions. We know that Mr. Praljak is going to testify. He has told us so many years ago already he is going to testify. From what I understood, when I read your submissions, I understand that you wanted to know what he was going to testify about. I looked at previous testimonies by several accused here at the Tribunal. It was my understanding that the accused did not let the Prosecution know beforehand what they were going to discuss during their testimony. I have a question mark here. Maybe you can shed some light on this, I don't know, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And let me just indicate right off the bat, I had an informal conversation with Mr. Kovacic before the proceedings started today, and he was kind enough to give us a bit of an advance preview of the intended witness order, and it's our understanding that General Praljak will be testifying at the beginning of the case in chief, so we do know that that is going to be the case. And you've correctly indicated, Mr. President, it's the Prosecution position that once the accused decides to take the stand that the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence then apply to that witness. He'll take the oath, and he'll be subject to cross-examination. The Rules that apply to any witness will apply in respect of General Praljak. So it's our view that in that situation, a summary should be provided in advance, and we'd certainly be grateful to the Praljak Defence were they to provide one to us, but that's certainly the position of the Prosecution; not only a witness summary, but then two weeks before the testimony begins, as is the case with other witnesses, the documents that the Defence would be using on the direct examination of General Praljak would also be provided or identified, not just for the Prosecution but for the other Defence teams as well. And of course, I can't speak for the other Defence teams, but they may also have a view, in terms of advance notice, both in terms of a witness summary and any documents that the Praljak team would be using on the direct examination. So that's our position on that question, Mr. President. And if I could add one last point. It is our intention to file a very -- it will be brief, but we will be filing a response to the notice that was filed by the Praljak Defence a few days ago about their proposed plan on having a supplemental Rule 84 bis statement or possibly a sworn statement of General Praljak in the nature of an opening statement, and I -- during our conversation before court, I informed Mr. Kovacic informally what I thought the Prosecution position would be in respect of that proposal or notice. But, in any event, here within the next couple of days, probably Wednesday or Thursday, since we're not here tomorrow, we will be filing a brief response to that notice to inform the Trial Chamber of our position on this issue of an opening statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I have an additional question to put to you. I did not quite understand whether General Praljak is going to testify before all your witnesses, or are the witnesses all going to testify and he will testify at the end, or Mr. Praljak will be testifying in the middle; you hear some witnesses first and some other witnesses after?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our plan, and we have had some informal talks about it, our plan is for Mr. Praljak to testify first. We will begin our case by calling him as a witness. After him, there will certainly be two expert witnesses. We have not yet completed our timetable for the remaining witnesses, which is why I told you I would prefer to wait for two or three days longer so that all the details will be correct, but we will certainly issue a schedule within a day or two, which will indicate that General Praljak will be the first witness, then two expert witnesses following him, and this will lead us to the last week of June. And then in the next two weeks, we will send the schedule for the remaining witnesses. As regards the questions or the issues raised by my learned friend, regardless of the practice at this Tribunal, we are now completing our job as regards this, and we intend to submit the summary of General Praljak's testimony and the documents that will be used during his examination-in-chief as soon as we can, which means that I believe we will be able to submit the summary by the 10th or 12th of April, certainly before the first half of April is over, and the documents four or five days later. So in any case, both the summary and the list of documents and the documents will be submitted long before a fortnight before the testimony begins, since according to the schedule, as it stands now, General Praljak will not be able to start testifying before the 6th of May. But we will certainly complete this task by the 15th of April, and, as I said, I hope that the summary will be ready around the 10th or 12th of April and the documents two or three days later. Regardless of what the practice is, we are guided by the principle of transparency, that we wish to be open and that we wish to enable our learned friends to prepare. We do not wish to conceal our hand, and we will simply make a selection of the documents. Thank you. Just as regards the proposal raised by the Prosecutor regarding Praljak's 84 bis statement, we did plan, as we informed the Chamber, for Mr. Praljak to make a statement under oath. We feel this is reasonable. He will tell the Court what he feels is important, and we will have to come back to many parts of that statement during his examination-in-chief. So that is the general information we wish to provide at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, as far as the submissions of the OTP are concerned, my attention was drawn on Mr. Blaskic's testimony, as I read everything. You have planned to hear this witness for two hours, and the Prosecutor feels that two hours is not very long. So what is it you had in mind, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is we who will call the witness, not the Prosecutor, so we will provide an estimate of the time we need in the schedule, which we will provide within the next two or three days. We are not obliged to examine any witness about every possible issue that the witness could be examined about or about every single thing contained in the witness's statement. We will question the witness about what we consider to be the most essential points and the most relevant points, in view of our limited time. Let me also inform Your Honours that all our witnesses, with one exception, have already given statements, and some might even be 92 bis witnesses, but when we call them as live witnesses and we have their statements, we will save time by asking the witness, in a relatively short space of time, about the most important points in the statement, and the rest of the statement, which we have in writing, we will submit as 92 ter testimony. I feel that this is a reasonable method, respecting the economy of the proceedings. And as far as I can recall, the OTP also used this method when putting forward their case, and we feel it's a rational and reasonable method. As regards Blaskic, for example, to what extent we will be putting questions in direct and how much will be covered by 92 bis is -- remains to be seen, but in our schedule we will certainly designate the amount of time that we now consider we will need. However, when we proof each witness, small changes may be made, small alterations. Is there any other information Your Honour requires?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I thank you, amongst other things, the fact that you want to make everybody's life easier. You indicated that you would send the summary of the examination-in-chief of your witnesses, as well as an exhibit list, as quickly as possible. As I am perfectly transparent and don't wish to take anybody by surprise either, I've been preparing myself for this testimony for some time now, and I intend to put my own questions for at least two hours. The other Judges on the Bench can do likewise. I will need two hours to put questions to General Praljak, and my outline will be what is contained in the indictment, so no surprise here. My questions will be in line with the indictment and in line with the documents mentioned in the footnote in the pre-trial brief and in other documents. So my questions will not come as a surprise, which will be entirely based on the indictment and the pre-trial brief and the pre-trial brief of General Praljak, which I have studied from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had something, because I'm afraid there may be a misunderstanding later on. It may also be a matter of interpretation. As regards the summaries of the remaining witnesses, we will provide a summary for Praljak, no question about that. As regards the summaries of the testimony of the other witnesses we will call live before this Court, the Defence of General Praljak has, for the most part, provided summaries in the 65 ter list we submitted in March last year, with perhaps two exceptions, and after that we gradually disclosed to the OTP and the other parties entire witness statements, far more than is contained in the summary. And according to the Rules, we are bound to provide the summary, so we have done this for all but two or three witnesses, and that is what the OTP motion concerns. And as I said, we will respond to it within two or three days, and Your Honours agreed to this. We will be responding to this. As regards Praljak, although there is no clear case law, we will provide a full and detailed summary. We do wish to provide this in advance to all parties, together with the documents, and it is our wish that Praljak be treated like any other witness as regards the technical aspects and the preparation for his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's very clear. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just two quick points. Counsel's made reference to Rule 92 ter, and the Trial Chamber will recall, because the procedure of 92 ter hasn't really been used -- I don't think it was used by the Prlic Defence or the Stojic Defence, as well, so we're coming back to a Rule that was used quite a bit during the Prosecution case but which has not been used a lot since then, and the Trial Chamber might recall that when the Prosecution called Rule 92 ter witnesses, obviously, because of the nature of how that Rule is applied, the Trial Chamber in advance generally tended to look at the statement and then to allocate time not only for the direct examination, if you will, but also tended to often -- very often allocate a greater amount of time for cross-examination of the 92 ter witness, because, of course, the direct testimony might be limited to a little part of the statement, but that the cross-examination, it was recognised, would have to cover the entirety of the written statement. So I just mention that now because it could impact the timing and the calender as we move into Rule 92 ter witnesses because the amount of time taken for the direct might well be exceeded in some cases significantly, possibly, and, for example, in the case of General Blaskic, if it turns out that he's tendered as a 92 witness. I don't know if that's going to be the case or not, but it may be that that additional time for cross could impact the calender at that stage of the trial. My second point is, and Mr. Kovacic just referred to the witness statements, the witness statements that the Prosecution has been provided, and while we're grateful for that, as we've said in our last submission, it's our position that a statement is not a substitute for a summary, a summary under Rule 65 ter, because a witness statement -- and Mr. Kovacic just mentioned this earlier. A statement can cover a lot of things, but it doesn't necessarily cover what will be the witness's testimony when the witness is in the box. The purpose of the summary is to enable all of the parties to have a much better idea of what the witness is actually going to say, and so the summary serves a different purpose, and it's our position that just because we've been provided with a witness statement, that does not excuse or diminish the responsibility of that same Defence team to submit a witness summary under Rule 65 ter that relates more specifically to what the witness is going to say when the witness is in the courtroom on direct, as opposed to what the witness might have talked about in a witness statement that he or she gave a long time ago. So that's our position on that, and we just wanted to state that so there is not confusion about the level to which we agree or disagree on the issue of witness statements and witness summaries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not respond now because we have to conclude. But as for this last issue raised by my learned friend, that is "sob judica" [phoen], because a motion has been filed. I'm duty-bound to file a response. You have agreed that I may do so by the end of the week, so I will not now respond. It's best for you to decide when you receive all the arguments in our written submissions. But as for the first part of what my learned friend has said regarding Rule 92 ter, I think that having checked what the practice and technology is, I don't see any -- anything that is in doubt here. Of course, it's up to Your Honours to decide what weight may be given to parts of the statement, but that is not a logistical problem. It's a problem -- it's something for Your Honours to decide. We can submit certain parts of the witness statement as 92 ter, and you may then decide that the OTP has two hours or two and a half hours to cross-examine. This has never been a problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm sure you'll be ever so happy to assist the Chamber, and while what you have outlined is quite correct, there is more time normally for cross when we have a 92 bis [sic] statement, it would of course be expected that you ask the Chamber for the amount of time you think you would need and justify this by giving reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minor error. It's not 92 bis, but 92 ter; page 38, line 25. Everything has been said. Ms. Nozica, on Wednesday, within 48 hours, you will have two witnesses. No problem with them?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on Wednesday we have one witness, and another on Thursday. That was our plan from the beginning, and unfortunately that's how we called our witnesses. While I could have done all this on Wednesday, but because of the situation around the court, the witness was unable to come tomorrow. He can come only the day after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I wish you all a very good afternoon. We shall reconvene on Wednesday at 9.00, since we're working in the mornings.
